name: COROIO
baseline: libevent (epoll backend; libevent commit 4c993a0, its bench.c methodology)
workload: libevent bench methodology: N pipe descriptors registered, then 1 active (or 100 active) connection passes 1-byte writes around the ring; p50 elapsed microseconds over 25 runs, epoll backend (coroio TEPoll vs libevent epoll), N from 1 to 131072.
claimed_speedup: No headline ratio in the README (results are charts); the raw result files in bench/ give p50 microseconds, lower is better. i7-12800H, 1 active connection, epoll: 64 us vs libevent 88 us at 1 descriptor (1.38x faster, derived from page data), 59 vs 92 at 4 descriptors (1.56x), 100 vs 95 at 1024 (coroio 5% slower), 110 vs 103 at 2048 (7% slower), 124 vs 129 at 131072 (parity). 100 active connections on the same CPU: 594 vs 955 us at 1 descriptor (1.61x), 879 vs 980 at 1024, but 1313 vs 1010 at 4096 and 1551 vs 1142 at 16384 (coroio 30-36% slower), parity at 65536 and above. i5-11400F (WSL2), 1 active, epoll: 47 vs 61 us at 1 descriptor, 78 vs 108 at 16384 (1.38x); 100 active: 1.17x to 1.74x faster across all sizes. Apple M1 kqueue, 1 active: 85 vs 100 us at 1 descriptor, 93 vs 137 at 16384 (1.47x). Separate actor-ring README table (i5-11400F, Ubuntu 25.04, author-run, against Akka, Caf and Ydb/actors rather than the listed baselines): local ring 442,151 msg/s vs Akka 473,966 (coroio slower), Caf 302,930, Ydb/actors 151,972; distributed ring 10 processes batch 1024 payload 0: 1,137,790 msg/s vs Ydb/actors 182,525, Caf 55,540, Akka 5,765.
compiler_and_flags: clang 16 on Ubuntu 23.04 for the i7-12800H run (README heading); optimization flags and CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE not stated (the repo's CMakeLists sets no default build type and only -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror on the library). Taskset pinned to CPU 10 with isolcpus/nohz_full per run.sh comments.
hardware: Intel Core i7-12800H (Ubuntu 23.04, performance governor, isolcpus=10,11); Intel Core i5-11400F under WSL2 kernel 6.1.21.1; Apple M1 MacBook Air 16 GB macOS 12.6.3.
stars_or_usage: 131 stars; used by miniraft-cpp and qumir (author's projects)
tradeoffs: Single-threaded event loop, C++23 required, coroutine frame allocation per task; pluggable backends (epoll, io_uring, kqueue, IOCP, poll, select). WebSocket is client-only, text frames only. No built-in multi-threading.
caveats: Author-run on three machines; first-party with partial methodology (flags and build type not stated), so tier C. Mixed result: on the i7-12800H libevent epoll is as fast or faster for 512 to 2048 descriptors with 1 active connection and coroio is 13-36% slower for 2048 to 32768 descriptors with 100 active connections; the clear wins are at small descriptor counts and on the i5-11400F and M1. The libevent side is libevent's own bench.c built as bench-libevent (build flags and the program source are not in the repo; run_libevent.sh takes the 12th smallest output line while coroio takes index 12 of 25 sorted runs, a one-rank difference if libevent prints one line per run). Both sides measure pipe event dispatch, not real socket echo or HTTP serving. No comparison against Boost.Asio or libuv exists in the repo. The actor-ring numbers use baselines outside the listed set and Akka is faster on the local ring. Charts in the README are images; the numbers above were read from bench/*.txt files and compared with a script (ratios derived from page data).

name: Envoy Proxy
baseline: NGINX 1.22.1 and HAProxy 2.7.3 as L7 reverse proxies
workload: Third-party Proxy-Benchmarks suite: hey, 100,000 GET requests at 250 concurrent connections from a client VM through each proxy to an echo-server backend, one run per proxy on AWS m5.xlarge instances (Envoy 1.22.8 default concurrency, NGINX worker_processes 3, HAProxy defaults).
claimed_speedup: Not faster on throughput. Envoy 25,852 req/s vs NGINX 33,506 and HAProxy 39,437 (Envoy 0.77x of NGINX and 0.66x of HAProxy, derived from page data); mean latency 9.5 ms vs 7.2 ms (NGINX) and 6.1 ms (HAProxy); p50 8.9 ms vs 5.7 and 4.1 ms. Lower tail only: p90 12.6 ms vs 14.7 (NGINX) and 13.8 (HAProxy), p95 13.9 vs 18.7 and 18.5, p99 19.5 ms vs 27.5 (NGINX) and 30.6 (HAProxy), i.e. 29% lower than NGINX and 36% lower than HAProxy at p99 (derived from page data). Envoy issue 5536 (wrk, 100 connections, 10 threads, 60 s, 4 workers each, nginx backend): Envoy 39,748.81 req/s, 2.73 ms average, 7.10 ms p99 vs HAProxy 88,446.34 req/s, 1.14 ms average, 2.20 ms p99.
compiler_and_flags: Not applicable: prebuilt container images (Envoy 1.22.8, NGINX 1.22.1, HAProxy 2.7.3, Caddy 2.6.4, Traefik 2.9.8) deployed with Terraform and Docker; no build flags.
hardware: AWS m5.xlarge for client, backend and proxy VMs (variables.tf default, us-east-2); CPU model not stated.
stars_or_usage: 29.1k stars; used as a sidecar proxy in service meshes (per the book lead)
tradeoffs: Broad feature set (filter chains, dynamic configuration, observability) gives up raw proxy speed in these runs; a contributor in issue 5536 attributes part of the gap to a relatively CPU-intensive HTTP/1 parser. Bazel build.
caveats: Envoy loses on throughput and on median and mean latency in both sources; the only favourable number is lower p90 to p99 latency in the Proxy-Benchmarks run. That run is one 100,000-request pass lasting 2.5 to 3.9 s per proxy, with the proxies configured differently (NGINX worker_processes 3, Envoy and HAProxy default threads on 4 vCPUs), no warm-up, and a hey client (coordinated omission possible). The repo was last updated Aug 2023 (313 stars) and tests Envoy 1.22.8, an old release. Issue 5536 is from 2019, hardware not stated, a maintainer-labelled question that was closed stale, and a commenter said the HAProxy config was not optimal. A 2020 HAProxy Technologies Kubernetes ingress benchmark and other write-ups showed in search snippets could not be opened (egress blocked), so they are not used. The Envoy README itself carries no comparison with NGINX or HAProxy.

name: OpenOnload (with ef_vi and TCPDirect kernel-bypass APIs)
baseline: Linux kernel UDP sockets (kernel network stack)
workload: UDP ping-pong with udpclient/udpserver from majek/dump (--polling --timestamp), client pinned with taskset -c 5, run natively and under the onload launcher, two back-to-back servers with Solarflare X2522 NICs, single channel, isolcpus and kernel tuning.
claimed_speedup: Average latency 14.303 us with Onload vs 20.310 us without (about 1.42x lower, derived from page data; a user reports 'an improvement of about ~3.5us'), packets per second 65540 vs 47340.
hardware: Two servers back-to-back with Solarflare X2522 NICs; CPU model, kernel and Onload version not stated.
tradeoffs: Best results need AMD Solarflare NICs (ef_vi native); other NICs use community-supported AF_XDP mode that is not release quality. Kernel modules plus a user-space library that intercepts socket calls, busy-polling cores (EF_POLL_USEC=100000 in the default latency profile per the issue), dual GPLv2.0 and BSD-2-Clause licensing, supported releases come from the vendor. ef_vi and TCPDirect require porting to their own APIs and, for ef_vi, a user-written protocol stack.
caveats: The only numbers reachable are a GitHub issue comment by a user (issue 28, 8 Mar 2022); no CPU model, kernel, Onload version or packet size, one run shown, so tier C. The same issue has another user reporting Onload about 1 us slower than kernel sockets on AWS ENA, and issue 139 (opened 20 Apr 2023, AWS m5zn.12xlarge, AF_XDP mode, custom UDP ping-pong) measured median 47.883 us with Onload vs 42.735 us with the kernel (Onload slower; a maintainer says latency is not expected to improve in AF_XDP mode, which targets epoll-heavy many-socket workloads). The README, README.ef_vi and the sibling TCPDirect README contain no numbers. Vendor user guide (UG1586) and the slide deck seen in a search snippet (reported ½ RTT TCP 11.2 us kernel vs 5.3 us Onload) could not be opened (host blocked); snippet only, not used for the tier. Benefit depends strongly on NIC, driver and tuning.

name: liburing4cpp
baseline: raw liburing C echo server (CarterLi/io_uring-echo-server, io_uring RECV-SEND); epoll echo server only indirectly
workload: TCP echo server driven by rust_echo_bench (cargo run --release), requests per second, three runs and median; C++ coroutine demo/echo_server vs the C io_uring echo server; plus a yield-path microbench (demo/bench) vs plain IORING_OP_NOP.
claimed_speedup: C++ coroutine echo server RECV-SEND median 120,239 req/s vs C 114,461, i.e. 105.05% of the C server's throughput (README column 'rate'). Other rows: POLL-RECV-SEND 111,210 (97.16% of the C RECV-SEND figure 114,461; C POLL-RECV-SEND is 114,893); SPLICE-SPLICE variants 77.84% to 81.63%. Yield microbench: service.yield 5436209973 vs plain IORING_OP_NOP 5268565967, 'About 3% overhead'.
compiler_and_flags: clang version 10.0.0-4ubuntu1 on Ubuntu 20.04.1, kernel 5.9.0-050900rc6; build flags for the measured binaries not stated (the README's load-tool command is cargo run --release; the CMake Release preset exists but is not tied to the numbers).
tradeoffs: Header-only binding needing a recent Linux kernel and liburing, C++20 coroutines; tasks are eagerly started (not lazy) and a dropped task does not cancel the kernel operation, so stack buffers can be written after scope exit.
caveats: The 105% is an abstraction-parity result against a raw io_uring C server written by the same author, not a win over epoll; 3 runs on one machine and the numbers appear to date from late 2020 (kernel 5.9.0-rc6 build of 2020-09-23, clang 10); the repo has been restructured since, and where the load generator ran is not stated. The C server (CarterLi/io_uring-echo-server) in its own README reports io_uring POLL-RECV-SEND at 106.70% (-c 50) and 101.79% (-c 200) of its epoll POLL-RECV-SEND server on a 4-vCPU VMware guest with clang 9.0.1, so the epoll comparison is indirect, run on different hardware, and within a few percent. The other C++ configurations (POLL, SPLICE) are slower than C, and the yield path is about 3% slower than plain NOP. Units for the yield microbench are not stated. First-party with flags not stated, so tier C.
